newsitem.title: CANADA: Inco seeks early maintenance at Sudbury.
newsitem.headline: Inco seeks early maintenance at Sudbury.

text.p: Inco Ltd said on Tuesday that it is seeking to start a regular summer shutdown and maintenance program at its Sudbury nickel mine as early as possible if the union will allow it.

Inco spokesman David Allen told Reuters the nickel-miner is in talks with its striking union workers in Sudbury to allow contract workers to perform maintenance work ahead of the mine's regular shutdown, which had been scheduled to start at end-June.
"We're discussing that possibility," said Inco's David Allen. "So we're discussing doing the maintenance, but we've also been asked by the union to return to the bargaining table."

Leaders of the United Steelworkers of America, representing Inco's 4,800 striking Sudbury workers, confirmed on Tuesday they had asked a provincial mediator to resume talks between the nickel giant and union leaders.

"Our committee wants to get to work and reach an agreement with the company. We have asked mediator (Dennis) Nelson to convey that message to Inco. The ball is now in their court," said Wayne Fraser, chief negotiator for the union's Local 6500.

Allen said he expects the union will grant Inco the opportunity to begin its shutdown maintenance early so that the Sudbury operation can be ready for production as soon as an agreement is struck between Inco and the strikers.
"It's to everybody's advantage that it be done," he said, noting that there is about a three week shutdown period in a normal schedule.
Allen also said Inco's refinery in Port Colborne, Ontario is still running. But he noted the refinery also handles materials from outside sources.
"As a general rule we don't keep any inventory that's not in process," said David Allen. "We have whatever was in process at the time production stopped, (but) I cannot get the number on that."
Allen noted that Inco's Acton, England refinery, which processes platinum and palladium, is operating normally. The Acton refinery also takes material from outside sources.
"If it doesn't have it from Sudbury it will have it from elsewhere," Allen said.
Inco's 4,670 unionized Sudbury workers went on strike at midnight on Monday, June 2, after voting 60.4 percent against a contract offer endorsed by union leaders.

Inco's Port Colborne, Ontario refinery, which processes cobalt, precious metals and electro-nickel, was not affected by the Sudbury strike. Unionized workers at the refinery approved the contract on Monday, June 2.
According to Inco's 1997 production plan, the Ontario division was expected to produce about 230 million pounds of nickel, about 200 million pounds of copper and about four million pounds of cobalt.
Inco spokesmen did not readily have production outlook figures for platinum group metals, but the company delivered 39,000 troy ounces in the first quarter 1997 and 294,000 troy ounces in 1996.
